entry: Marine [[Echinoderm|echinoderm]] of the class Asteroidea, usually with five arms radiating from a central disc. Starfish, also called sea stars, are found in all the world's oceans. About 1,900 species live on the seabed, from intertidal zones to abyssal depths of 6,000 m (20,000 ft). They have tube feet operated by a hydraulic system and a mouth at the center of the lower surface. Starfish are opportunistic feeders, mostly predators of benthic invertebrates, and most can regenerate damaged parts or lost arms. Some species, such as the ochre sea star (*Pisaster ochraceus*), are keystone species with an outsize impact on their environment. The crown-of-thorns starfish (*Acanthaster planci*) is a voracious predator of [[Coral|coral]] across the Indo-Pacific. The fossil record reaches back to the [[Ordovician]] period, about 450 million years ago, but is sparse because starfish tend to disintegrate after death.

American military science fiction franchise, owned by Amazon MGM Studios. It began with the 1994 film *Stargate*, directed by Roland Emmerich, which was released by [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]]. Its premise is a ring-shaped device, the Stargate, that allows travel across vast distances via [[Wormhole|wormholes]]. The television series *Stargate SG-1* (1997) was joined by *Stargate Atlantis* (2004) and *Stargate Universe* (2009), which ended in 2011. Related books, video games, comics and direct-to-DVD films extend the story. The main story arc ran for more than 15 years, including 18 seasons (364 episodes).

Family of small to medium-sized [[Passerine|passerine]] birds, noted for iridescent plumage, vocal mimicry and elaborate flock displays called murmurations. The family Sturnidae is named for the genus *Sturnus*, from the Latin word *sturnus* for starling, and contains 128 species in 36 genera. Many Asian species, particularly the larger ones, are called mynas, and many African species are known as glossy starlings. Starlings are native to Europe, Asia, Africa, northern Australia and the islands of the tropical Pacific. Several European and Asian species have been introduced to [[North America]], [[Hawaii]] and [[New Zealand]], where they compete with native birds and are considered [[Invasive species|invasive]]. Most species nest in holes and lay blue or white eggs. Starlings can embed sounds from their surroundings, including car alarms and human speech, into their calls.

Religion or creed endorsed by a sovereign state. A state with an official religion, also called a confessional state, is not necessarily a [[Theocracy|theocracy]]. Official religions have existed in almost all cultures throughout human history, reaching into the Ancient Near East and prehistory. They generally enjoy more rights and fewer restrictions than other faiths. The degree of state backing varies, from mere endorsement with freedom for other faiths to prohibiting competing bodies and persecuting other sects. In England, [[Henry VIII]] broke with Rome in 1534 and was declared Supreme Head of the [[Church of England]]. In contemporary societies, the imposition of an official religion ranges from high in [[Saudi Arabia]] and [[Iran]] to none at all in Greenland, Denmark, England, Iceland and Greece.

First-level administrative subdivisions of Germany, known in German as *Länder*. The sixteen states are partly sovereign. Thirteen are area-states, in which counties and county-level cities have their own administration. [[Berlin]] and [[Hamburg]] are [[City-state|city-states]], and Bremen is a mixture of a city-state and an area-state. [[Bavaria]], [[Saxony]] and [[Thuringia]] call themselves *Freistaat* ("free state"), a stylistic title with no legal significance. In 1952, Baden, Württemberg-Baden and Württemberg-Hohenzollern merged into [[Baden-Württemberg]]. In 1957, the Saar Protectorate joined as [[Saarland]]. German reunification in 1990 added five eastern states, and East and West Berlin reunited as a city-state.

Imbalance of electric charges within or on the surface of a material. The charge remains until it moves away as an [[Electric current|electric current]] or by electrical discharge. The word "static" distinguishes it from current electricity, in which charge flows through a conductor. Electrons may move between two materials on contact or sliding, leaving one positively charged and the other negatively charged; this triboelectric effect is the main cause of everyday static. A static shock is an electrostatic discharge, the neutralization of a charge when it reaches a conductor or an oppositely charged region.

Branch of [[Classical mechanics|classical mechanics]] concerned with [[Force|forces]] and [[Torque|torques]] acting on systems in equilibrium. Statics analyzes systems that do not accelerate: they are either at rest or their center of mass moves at constant velocity. Zero acceleration means the total force is zero, and the summation of moments, which equals the moment of inertia times angular acceleration, is also zero. Together, these two "conditions for equilibrium" can be used to solve for unknown quantities acting on a system. A force is either a push or a pull, with magnitude, direction and point of application. The moment of a force, also called torque, equals the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the axis to its line of action. [[Archimedes]] did pioneering work in statics.

Automobile body style, a variant of the [[Sedan (automobile)|sedan]] with its roof extended rearward over a shared passenger and cargo area. Access is at the back through a third or fifth door, or tailgate, instead of a trunk lid. Fold-down rear seats let the interior favor passengers or cargo. Early wagons carried people and luggage to and from a [[Train station|train station]]; the style is called a "wagon" in the United States and an "estate car" in the United Kingdom. Demand has faded since the 2010s in favor of [[SUV]] and crossover designs, especially in the United States and Canada.

Method of statistical inference for deciding whether data provide sufficient evidence to reject a particular hypothesis. The test typically computes a test statistic, then decides by comparing it with a critical value or by evaluating the [[P-value|p-value]] computed from it. The null hypothesis (H₀), usually a statement of "no effect" or "no difference," is tested against the alternative hypothesis (H₁). If the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level (α), the null hypothesis is rejected, but the test does not conclude that it is false. Conclusions are never certain. A type I error rejects a true null hypothesis, with probability α, while a type II error accepts it when the alternative is true, with probability β. The power of a test, 1−β, measures its ability to detect a true alternative. Roughly 100 specialized statistical tests are in use.

Branch of [[Physics|physics]] that applies statistical methods and probability theory to large assemblies of microscopic entities. Also called statistical physics or statistical thermodynamics, it aims to clarify the properties of matter in aggregate, in terms of physical laws governing atomic motion. It arose from classical [[Thermodynamics|thermodynamics]], explaining properties such as temperature, pressure and heat capacity in terms of microscopic parameters described by probability distributions. Its applications extend to chemical reactions, neuroscience, computer science, information theory and sociology. Non-equilibrium statistical mechanics models the speed of irreversible processes driven by imbalances, such as flows of particles and heat. The field is generally credited to [[Ludwig Boltzmann]], [[James Clerk Maxwell]] and [[Josiah Willard Gibbs]], and Gibbs coined the name in 1884.

Set of similar items of interest for some question or experiment. A statistical population can be a group of existing objects, such as all stars within the [[Milky Way]], or a hypothetical, potentially infinite group, such as all possible hands in a game of poker. In statistical inference, the population is modeled by a [[Probability distribution|probability distribution]] with unknown parameters. By analyzing a [[Sampling (statistics)|sample]], these parameters can be estimated using appropriate sample statistics. The population mean is the arithmetic mean of a numerical property across the entire population, or the [[Expected value|expected value]] when the property is a random variable. Not every distribution has a well-defined mean; the Cauchy distribution is an example. The [[Law of large numbers|law of large numbers]] states that the larger the sample, the more likely its mean is to be close to the population mean.

Colossal neoclassical sculpture of a robed, crowned woman on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. Officially titled *Liberty Enlightening the World*, it depicts Libertas, the Roman goddess of liberty, holding a torch and a tablet inscribed with the date of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Designed by French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, its metal framework was built by [[Gustave Eiffel]]. The [[Copper|copper]]-clad statue was a gift from the people of France to the United States and was dedicated on October 28, 1886, by President [[Grover Cleveland]]. Édouard de Laboulaye proposed the monument in 1865 to commemorate the centennial of U.S. independence. Fundraising in America was driven by publisher [[Joseph Pulitzer]] of the *New York World*. The statue became a symbol of welcome to immigrants arriving by sea. Since 1933 it has been maintained by the National Park Service.

World's tallest statue, 182 meters (597 feet) high, depicting Indian independence leader [[Vallabhbhai Patel|Sardar Patel]]. It stands near Kevadia, Gujarat, on the Narmada River, and was designed by sculptor Ram V. Sutar. Construction began in October 2013 and cost ₹27 billion (US$422 million). [[Narendra Modi]] inaugurated it on 31 October 2018, on what would have been Patel's 143rd birthday. The statue is built to withstand winds of up to 180 kilometers per hour and earthquakes measuring 6.5 on the [[Richter scale]].

Law or formal written enactment of a [[Legislature|legislature]]. Statutes typically declare, command or prohibit something. They are distinguished from [[Common law|common law]], which is unwritten, and from secondary legislation, or regulations, issued by an executive body under authority granted by a statute. Depending on the legal system, a statute may be called an "act." The word appears in English as early as the 14th century, derived from Old French *statut*. Many countries organize statutes into topical codes, which are amended as new statutes add, amend or repeal sections. In many nations, statutory law is subordinate to [[Constitution|constitutional law]]. The term also covers treaties establishing institutions, such as the Statute of the [[International Court of Justice]]. In Spain, an autonomy statute resembles a constitution and has the rank of organic law.

Process by which courts interpret and apply legislation. Some interpretation is often necessary, because a statute's ambiguous words must be resolved by the judge. Judges use traditional canons of construction, legislative history and purpose. In [[Common law|common law]] jurisdictions, the same rules may apply to delegated legislation such as administrative agency regulations. English courts developed three main rules, the mischief rule, the literal rule and the golden rule, all aimed at the "intention of Parliament." Courts also presume that statutes do not change the common law, remove individual liberty or property, or apply retrospectively. Textualism prioritizes the ordinary public meaning of words, while purposivism infers meaning from a statute's objectives. The two approaches remain contested, particularly over the use of legislative history.

Sexual activity with a person below the [[Age of consent|age of consent]]. The term usually refers to adults engaging in sexual contact with minors. Overt force or threat is usually absent, because the law presumes coercion: a minor or mentally disabled adult is incapable of consent. In many jurisdictions the age of consent means mental or functional age, so a victim may be of any chronological age. In Italy the age of consent is 14, with a "Romeo and Juliet" rule for a one-year age difference, rising to 16 where the older person has authority, such as a teacher or doctor.

Military techniques that make personnel, aircraft, ships and vehicles less detectable to [[Radar|radar]], infrared, [[Sonar|sonar]] and other sensors. Also termed low observable technology, stealth is a sub-discipline of military tactics that corresponds to multispectral [[Camouflage|camouflage]]. Development of modern stealth in the United States began in 1958, after attempts to prevent [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] radar tracking of U-2 spy planes had failed. Designers shaped aircraft to redirect radar waves and applied radiation-absorbent material, producing the Northrop Grumman B-2 Spirit "Stealth Bomber." Methods of visual concealment were documented by [[Sun Tzu]] in *The Art of War* in the 5th century BC. In 1916 the British modified an airship for night reconnaissance, but its silent, dark design produced little useful intelligence. The concept of stealth is to operate or hide from external observation, and the degree of stealth in a design is chosen according to the projected threats of detection.

Locomotive that moves itself and other vehicles by the expansion of [[Steam engine|steam]], also called an iron horse. It burns [[Coal|coal]], [[Coke (fuel)|coke]], oil or, rarely, wood to heat water in its boiler, where the water's volume increases 1,600 to 1,700 times. Richard Trevithick built the first locomotive known to have hauled a load over a distance, at Pen-y-darren in 1804. *Locomotion No. 1*, built by [[George Stephenson]] and his son Robert, hauled passengers on a public railway, the Stockton and Darlington Railway, in 1825. Steam locomotives were superseded by electric and diesel locomotives from the early 1900s, and most were retired by the 1980s, though several continue on tourist and heritage lines. A British speed record of 126 miles per hour (203 kilometers per hour), still unbroken, was set by LNER Class A4 4468 *Mallard*.

Digital distribution platform for PC games, developed by [[Valve Corporation|Valve]]. Launched as a software client in September 2003 to update Valve's games automatically, it expanded to third-party titles in late 2005. Features include cloud storage, direct messaging and community forums. Steamworks, an [[API|application programming interface]] released in 2008, lets developers integrate Steam's functions, including digital rights management. The platform was ported to [[MacOS|macOS]] in 2010 and to [[Linux]] in 2013. As of 2013 it held an estimated 75% of the PC game distribution market; by 2021 it offered over 34,000 games and over 132 million monthly active users.

Heat engine that extracts thermal energy from pressurized steam to do mechanical work through a rotating output shaft. Its modern form was invented by Sir Charles Parsons in 1884, and it revolutionized marine propulsion. Much of its efficiency comes from multiple stages in the expansion of steam. Because it generates rotary motion, it can drive an [[Electric generator|electric generator]], forming the core of thermal [[Power station|power stations]] fueled by fossil fuels, nuclear fuels, geothermal or solar energy. About 42% of all U.S. electricity generation in 2022 came from steam turbines. The largest ever built is the 1,770 MW Arabelle, two units of which will be installed at Hinkley Point C Nuclear Power Station. Technical challenges include rotor imbalance, vibration and bearing wear.

Cooking method in which food is fully immersed in steam with no air present, so that the steam condenses on the food. It is often done in a food steamer, or in a wok. Some of the world's earliest steam cookers, made of stoneware, have been found in China's [[Yellow River]] valley, dating back to as early as 5,000 BCE. Steaming is considered a healthy technique and can be far faster and more energy-efficient than full immersion in [[Boiling|boiling water]], because it heats much less water. A 2007 USDA comparison found that steaming reduces [[Vitamin C|vitamin C]] by 15%, and boiling reduces it by 25%. Bamboo steamers take longer to heat up but absorb excess moisture.

Steam-powered vessel, typically ocean-faring, propelled by steam engines that turn propellers or paddlewheels. Steamships were preceded by smaller steamboats; the first working steamboat and paddle steamer, the *Pyroscaphe*, dates from 1783. Paddlewheels were standard on early vessels, but their performance fell when added weight submerged them. The change to the screw propeller made ocean-going steamers viable. The first steamship purpose-built for regular trans-Atlantic crossings, the side-wheel paddle steamer *Great Western*, was built by [[Isambard Kingdom Brunel]] in 1838 and inaugurated the era of the trans-Atlantic [[Ocean liner|ocean liner]]. In 1839, *Archimedes* became the first screw propeller-driven steamship for open-water seagoing. Because steamships depended less on wind patterns, new trade routes opened, and the steamship has been described as a major driver of the first wave of [[Globalization|trade globalization]] (1870–1913).

Process of producing [[Steel|steel]] from iron ore and/or scrap. Steel is made from iron and carbon, with less than 1 percent carbon giving it strength. Impurities such as nitrogen, silicon, phosphorus and sulfur are removed, and alloying elements such as manganese, nickel, chromium and vanadium are added to produce different grades. Two major commercial processes are used. Basic oxygen steelmaking (BOS) uses liquid [[Pig iron|pig iron]] from a blast furnace and scrap steel as its main feed, while electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking uses scrap steel or direct reduced iron. Oxygen steelmaking has become more popular over time. Commercialized on a massive scale in the 1850s and 1860s by the Bessemer and Siemens-Martin processes, steelmaking is one of the most carbon-intensive industries. In 2020 it was responsible for 7% of energy sector greenhouse gas emissions.

American rock band formed in 1971 by Walter Becker and Donald Fagen in Annandale-on-Hudson, New York. Becker and Fagen stopped performing live by the end of 1974 and continued as a studio-only duo. Their music blended rock, [[Jazz|jazz]], Latin, R&B and [[Blues|blues]] with cryptic, irony-infused lyrics. Their top-selling album, *Aja*, came out in 1977. The band disbanded in 1981 and reunited in 1993. It was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2001 and has sold more than 40 million records. After Becker's death in 2017, Fagen remained the sole official member until 2024.

Polish mathematician, one of the founders of modern [[Functional analysis|functional analysis]]. Banach was an original member of the [[Lviv|Lwów]] School of Mathematics. With Hugo Steinhaus, he established the Polish Mathematical Society in 1919 and later published the journal *Studia Mathematica*. His major work was the 1932 book *Théorie des opérations linéaires* (*Theory of Linear Operations*), the first monograph on the general theory of functional analysis. Concepts bearing his name include Banach spaces, Banach algebras, the Banach–Tarski paradox, the Hahn–Banach theorem and the Banach fixed-point theorem. He became a professor at the Lwów Polytechnic in 1922 and a member of the Polish Academy of Learning in 1924.
